metric.why: Two facilities with identical PUE differ enormously in carbon depending on the grid feeding them. CUE is how siting decisions and power purchase agreements show up in a single operational number.
metric.formula: Total CO2 emissions from facility energy / IT energy in kWh
metric.definition: Kilograms of carbon dioxide emitted, from the grid mix and on-site generation, per kilowatt-hour of IT energy.

reading.body:
CUE makes grid carbon visible at the facility level: a data center with excellent power efficiency can still carry a high CUE if the grid feeding it is carbon-intensive, and a less efficient building on a clean grid can score better.

PUE, the older and more familiar metric, measures how much energy is lost to cooling and overhead before it reaches servers. CUE starts where PUE leaves off. It takes whatever total energy the facility consumes, from both the grid and any on-site generation, and weights it by the carbon intensity of those sources. Two facilities that look identical on PUE can differ enormously on CUE. That difference is determined by siting and by the power purchase agreements the operator has signed, not by anything inside the building.

For AI infrastructure specifically, this matters because training and inference workloads are geographically mobile in a way that, say, a hospital is not. The choice of where to build or lease capacity is also a choice about carbon per kilowatt-hour of compute. CUE is the number that makes that trade-off legible in operations rather than only in procurement documents.

The data here covers CUE as a defined metric and explains its formula and purpose. It does not provide CUE values for any specific facility, operator, or grid region, and it does not address how CUE interacts with the water or renewable-energy metrics listed alongside it. Those questions are outside what this entry contains.
